1.pericope_label: And king Zedekiah the son of Josiah reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, whom Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah
debates: Why the deposed king name is shortened
Whether the king request for prayer was sincere
What the errand of the two messengers was
outliers: Gill reports from Jarchi that Jehoiakim was wicked while his people were righteous and Zedekiah righteous while his people were wicked, and objects that the character rests on a single act, since king and people alike were corrupt

Henry refuses to make the request for prayer mere hypocrisy, commending it as a sign of some good in the king, while noting that it condemns him out of his own mouth, since it is common for those to desire to be prayed for who will not be advised

Ellicott suspects the two messengers, who belonged to the party opposed to submission, were trying to win the prophet over by a show of religious zeal, and finds the stress they lay on praying to the Lord our God the likelier explanation
themes: A three months reign reckoned as nothing
A name clipped short by way of reproach
Sending for prayers while refusing counsel
Men who seek God without earnestness

4.pericope_label: Then Pharaoh army was come forth out of Egypt: and when the Chaldeans that besieged Jerusalem heard tidings of them, they departed from Jerusalem
debates: When in the siege the messengers were sent
Why the Egyptian army turned back
What the king was really asking for
outliers: Calvin distinguishes the faithful, who ask others to pray and still pray themselves, from the hypocrite, who thinks access forbidden him and substitutes another in his place without praying at all
Clarke says the Egyptians were defeated and returned at once, not being hearty in the cause, while Calvin leaves the cause open, whether beaten in battle or merely struck with fear

Calvin observes that the reply speaks of the king sending to inquire though the errand named was prayer, and concludes he wanted a favourable oracle as well, asking why he applied to this man rather than the chief priest unless he knew him to be a true prophet
themes: A liberty that lasted only until the next answer
Everything hanging on one uncertain battle
A man who wants the world to pray for him and never prays
Relief that only suspended the siege

9.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart
debates: Why a second warning was needed
Why only the burning is mentioned and not the assault
Why the prophet tried to leave the city
outliers: Calvin explains that the warning was added because the king might have hardened under the first answer, as hypocrites do who on finding they can gain nothing become furious and run headlong on

Calvin argues from the omission of any assault that no valour or skill is needed to burn a city, a thing women and children have done to whole towns, so that men lying half dead are strong enough once God has armed them

Henry reads the attempt to leave as a settled decision rather than a flight, since the prophet found he could do no good in the city, and holds that there are times when it is the wisdom of good men to retire into privacy
themes: A hope that was never real
The instruments little regarded once the effect is resolved
A man of eminence content to be lost in a crowd
Wounded men without banner or comrade

12.pericope_label: Then Jeremiah went forth out of Jerusalem to go into the land of Benjamin, to separate himself thence in the midst of the people
debates: What the prophet meant to do in Benjamin
Why the charge of desertion was brought
Whether the accusation had any plausibility
outliers: Ellicott and Clarke both take the errand as a matter of property, a priest of Anathoth going to plough or to draw his share of produce, while Calvin calls the heritage reading harsh and forced and prefers that he sought a quiet place among his own people

Clarke reports the property reading from Blayney and the agreement of the Chaldee, and sets against it the rendering of Dahler, that he went to withdraw himself from the siege as other inhabitants did
Keil and Delitzsch grant the accusation was founded on the prophet well-known views but call it mere sophistry, since the enemy were no longer lying before the city at all
themes: A gate that stood open only because the siege had lifted
A prediction turned into evidence of treason
A name worth more than a life to wise men
Calumny that no care can wholly prevent

15.pericope_label: Wherefore the princes were wroth with Jeremiah, and smote him, and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe: for they had made that the prison
debates: What kind of place the prison was
Where the sentence about the dungeon belongs
What the king was asking for
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch break with most interpreters by refusing to attach the verse about the dungeon to what precedes, since the resulting sentence would be long and lumbering and the clause stands too far from the verb

Calvin cannot see why some render the word for the cells as victualling houses, and prefers the explanation that makes them niches scooped near the bottom of a pit so prisoners could lodge without sinking into the mire

Calvin is careful to say the king was not among the worst, since he sent of his own accord, but describes the usual way of hypocrites, who would be reconciled to God and remain free at once, wanting him to give place to them
themes: A trial where wrath left no room for equity
Princes who smote by ordering others to smite
A cell too narrow to sit or stand in
A prisoner who would not soften one word to his gaoler

18.pericope_label: Moreover Jeremiah said unto king Zedekiah, What have I offended against thee, or against thy servants, or against this people, that ye have put me in prison
debates: Whether a subject may deny wrongdoing against a king
What the state of the false prophets credit was
Why the ration is described so precisely
outliers: Calvin holds that princes are not absolved before God merely because they will not bear their decrees disregarded, and that a man may openly assert his innocence when religion constrains him and it is not lawful to obey an impious edict

Gill marks the change of register, that the prophet spoke in the name of the Lord with boldness and majesty and for himself with the submission proper to a subject, owning as sovereign a prince whose destruction he knew was at hand

Calvin makes the meanness of the ration a mercy, since at home the prophet might have been stoned or robbed, while in prison he was safe and fed when he could not have got bread by labour or begging or money
themes: Decrees counted sacred by men who make them
A true prophet in prison and false ones in the palace
Prophets who were not logs of wood
A city with a street for every trade
